column8: Welcome to Battles of History. Today we are learning about the Battle of Tah-lahs, which happened in July 751, between the army of Tang China and the army of the Ab-bah-sid Caliphate.

Battle of Tah-lahs. In July 751, in a river valley in the middle of Asia, the army of Tang China met the army of the Ab-bah-sid Caliphate. It was the only major battle known between the armies of Tang China and the Arab Caliphate. Very little was written about it at the time. This introduction separates what the sources say from what historians have pieced together. Watch the colour of each tag.

Two empires. In 751 Tang China was at the height of its power. From its western headquarters at Koo-cha, the Protectorate of Ahn-shee, its generals watched over the oasis kingdoms of the Silk Road as far as the mountains of Central Asia. Far to the west a new power had just risen. In 750 the Ab-bah-sid family overthrew the Oo-my-yad caliphs, with an army raised in Khoo-rah-sahn, in eastern Iran, under the black banners of Ah-boo Muslim. Its commanders were extending their authority across Khoo-rah-sahn and the contested cities of Trans-ox-ee-ah-na, including Samarkand and Bukhara. Between them lay the cities of the Sog-dee-ans, merchants of the Silk Road, and the pastures of the Turkic peoples, who took sides as it suited them.

The spark. The Chinese histories say that in 750 the Tang general Gow Shyen-jur made peace with the king of Chahch, the city that is Tashkent today, then broke his word, seized the city and sent the king to the Chinese capital, Chahng-ahn, where he was put to death. The king's son escaped and told neighbouring rulers what Gow had done. The Chinese histories say they then invited the Arabs to attack the Tang garrisons. The Arab historian Ibn al-Ah-theer tells it differently: the ruler of Fer-gah-na asked the Chinese for help against the ruler of Chahch, and Ah-boo Muslim answered the Chinese intervention.

The armies. Gow Shyen-jur led thirty thousand Tang and allied soldiers, according to the Comprehensive Mirror. Other Chinese accounts give twenty or sixty thousand, while Arab accounts give much larger figures. Its core was the professional army of Ahn-shee, with armoured infantry and crossbows, under hard veterans like the general Lee Suh-yeh. With them marched allies from the kingdom of Fer-gah-na, and the Kar-looks, a Turkic people. The Ab-bah-sid army was commanded by Zee-yahd ibn Sah-lih, sent by Ah-boo Muslim from Khoo-rah-sahn. No reliable figure for its size survives. Modern estimates vary widely, and none can be confirmed.

The sources. The Chinese sources include the two Tang histories and the Comprehensive Mirror. Doo Yo's Tong-dyen also preserves passages from the travel account of his relative Doo Hwahn, who was captured. The Arabic accounts are brief and sometimes tell a different story, especially about why the armies fought and how many men were lost. No source describes how the armies stood or what happened on each of the five days. In this reenactment, those parts are our reconstruction, and they are marked as such.

The ground. Ancient Tah-rahz, the town of Tah-lahs, stood near the site of modern Tah-rahz in Kazakhstan. The battle took place somewhere in the surrounding Tah-lahs valley. The exact battlefield has never been found. The Arab writers name the place At-lahk. Historians and archaeologists in Kazakhstan and Kyrgyzstan place it on the plain south of Tah-rahz, and Kyrgyzstan raised a monument there in 2021. The maps in this reenactment are drawn from real satellite measurements of the valley. Where the armies stood on them is our reconstruction.

Gow marched west from Ahn-shee toward Tah-lahs. His exact route is unknown; he may have crossed the Tyen Shahn and passed near Ee-sik Kool. The Comprehensive Mirror says he marched more than seven hundred lee into enemy territory. The exact distance in modern kilometres is uncertain.

The Chinese account says Gow heard that the western rulers and the Arabs might attack the Ahn-shee garrisons, and he marched west to confront them first. It was the way he had always fought: in 747 he had crossed the Pamirs to take a Tibetan-held kingdom by surprise.
Zee-yahd ibn Sah-lih leads the Ab-bah-sid army toward Tah-lahs. His exact route is unknown, but he brings forces from the western lands to confront Gow.

The Ab-bah-sids had only just won their civil war, and Ah-boo Muslim, who ruled the east for them, was still putting down rebels. Sending an army to the Tah-lahs shows how seriously he took the Tang advance. The Arab sources say little more than that Zee-yahd met the Chinese and defeated them.
The armies meet in the Tah-lahs valley. Gow has advanced from the Tang frontier, while Zee-yahd has come from the Ab-bah-sid-controlled lands to the west.

Tah-lahs was a Silk Road town on the edge of the steppe. The Chinese pilgrim Shwen-dzahng had passed through it in 630, and it had once acknowledged the Tang. To fight there was to fight on the old border between the Chinese world and the lands of Islam.
The armies form their lines on the plain. We show Tang crossbowmen and heavy infantry at the centre, with allied horsemen on the wings.
No source records the battle formations. These positions are based on known Tang weapons and military practice, but they remain a reconstruction.
Fighting begins between the two armies. We imagine cavalry attacks and volleys of crossbow bolts, but the sources do not tell us how the first day unfolded.
Tang armies used crossbows and disciplined infantry. The Ab-bah-sids also had experienced soldiers, but neither side's exact tactics at Tah-lahs are recorded.
The Comprehensive Mirror says the two armies faced each other for five days. We do not know how much fighting took place on each day.
Five days of confrontation suggests a difficult contest, but the sources do not tell us what either commander was planning or waiting for.
After five days, the Kar-looks turn against the Tang. The Chinese account says they and the Ab-bah-sids attack Gow's army from two sides, causing its defeat.

The Chinese account says the Kar-looks rebelled against Gow. Their exact allegiance before the battle, and whether their attack was planned, remain disputed. The Kar-looks had their own political interests in the region; why they chose to attack Gow's army is not recorded.
Gow's army suffers a crushing defeat. The Comprehensive Mirror says only a few thousand survive. The Arabic tradition also reports large numbers of prisoners.

The Chinese accounts describe a devastating defeat, with only a few thousand survivors. Ibn al-Ah-theer claims fifty thousand killed and twenty thousand captured, figures far above the Chinese army totals. Gow's expeditionary army was shattered, although some survivors returned to Ahn-shee and Tang military power there continued.
Lee Suh-yeh urges Gow Shyen-jur to withdraw toward White Stone Ridge. Gow first wants to gather his survivors and fight again, but Lee Suh-yeh persuades him to retreat.
The Old and New Histories of the Tang both name White Stone Ridge, but its exact location is unknown. We cannot place it confidently on a modern map.
The narrow road is blocked by retreating Fer-gah-na troops, their horses and camels. Lee Suh-yeh forces a passage with a great club, killing men and animals so Gow can escape.
Lee Suh-yeh was a powerful infantry commander, famous for using the heavy mo-dow blade. The Tang histories admired his fighting ability, even while recording this brutal escape.
A junior officer, Dwahn Shyo-shur, rebukes Lee Suh-yeh for abandoning his men. Lee Suh-yeh apologizes, then stays behind to resist pursuit and gather scattered survivors.
Lee Suh-yeh accepted Duan's rebuke. After returning to Ahn-shee, he recommended Duan for a military appointment. Both men later served during the Ahn Loo-shahn rebellion.

Many Tang soldiers were reportedly captured, and some were taken west into Ab-bah-sid territory. One of the captives was Doo Hwahn, who had accompanied Gow's expedition. After travelling through the Ab-bah-sid world, he returned to China by merchant ship in 762.

Nearly three centuries later, al-Thah-ah-lee-bee wrote that Chinese prisoners from Tah-lahs brought paper-making to Samarkand. But paper was already known in Central Asia, so the story cannot be accepted as the origin of the craft there.
Gow Shyen-jur returns from Tah-lahs with survivors. His career continues, and he later receives another major command when rebellion threatens the Tang dynasty.
Tah-lahs was a severe military defeat, but it did not immediately end Tang control of the western garrisons. A much greater crisis followed four years later.

In 755 Ahn Loo-shahn rebelled against the Tang. Troops from the western frontier were drawn into the struggle. In early 756 Gow Shyen-jur was executed on his own emperor's orders after accusations against him.
Tah-lahs mattered politically, but it did not decide Central Asia's religion. Islam spread over centuries through trade, political change, conversion and, at times, conquest.

The Ab-bah-sid army defeated Gow Shyen-jur's Tang forces after a five-day confrontation. The Chinese account says the Kar-looks turned against Gow and helped defeat him. Chinese accounts give different army sizes, from twenty to sixty thousand. The Comprehensive Mirror uses thirty thousand and says only a few thousand survived. Doo Hwahn was captured and spent more than a decade in the Ab-bah-sid world. He returned to China by sea in 762 and wrote about his experiences. The battle did not end Chinese power in Central Asia. The Ahn Loo-shahn rebellion of 755 did.
